# How Naira Devaluation and Inflation Affect Your Investments


**In short:** Inflation and a weaker naira both erode what your money can buy, so cash left idle loses value over time. Nigeria’s inflation was 15.91% in mid-2026, and the naira has fallen from around ₦460 to the dollar in 2023 to roughly ₦1,400. Investing across both naira and dollar assets is how many Nigerians try to protect their purchasing power, though returns are never guaranteed.


Ask anyone in Nigeria what has changed about money in the last few years and you will hear the same thing: it does not go as far as it used to. The ₦10,000 that filled a basket of groceries in 2022 does not fill it today. That feeling has a name, actually two, and understanding them is the difference between watching your money quietly shrink and doing something about it.


This guide explains what inflation and naira devaluation are, how they quietly erode the value of money left sitting still, what they mean for your investments, and how Nigerians respond to both. It is general information, not investment advice. If you are new to investing altogether, our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) is a good starting point.


## What do inflation and devaluation actually mean for your money?


Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over time, which means each naira buys a little less than it did before. Devaluation is the fall in the naira’s value against other currencies, especially the US dollar, which makes imported goods and foreign currency more expensive in naira terms. They are different forces, but they push in the same direction: your money loses purchasing power.


Both have been severe in Nigeria recently. Inflation reached 15.91% in June 2026, according to[National Bureau of Statistics data reported](https://www.channelstv.com/2026/07/15/nigerias-inflation-rate-drops-slightly-from-15-93-to-15-91-in-june/) at the time, easing from around 25% a year earlier but still high. On the currency side, after the naira was floated in June 2023, it fell from roughly ₦460 to the dollar to well over ₦1,400, as[reporting on the naira’s trajectory](https://punchng.com/nairas-tumultuous-trajectory/) has tracked. In plain terms, money held in naira buys far less abroad, and far less at home, than it did three years ago.


## Why cash quietly loses value


Money left sitting in cash or a low-interest account loses value in real terms whenever inflation runs higher than the interest you earn on it. This is the part most people feel but do not name.


Here is the mechanism. If your savings earn, say, 8% a year while prices rise by around 16%, your money is growing on paper but shrinking in what it can actually buy. The gap between the two is your real loss. Economists call the return after inflation your “real return,” and when inflation is higher than your interest rate, that real return is negative. You have more naira and less power to spend it.


Devaluation compounds this for anything tied to foreign currency. School fees abroad, imported electronics, medical trips, foreign software subscriptions, and even locally sold goods with imported components all cost more in naira as the currency weakens. So the same savings lose ground twice: once to rising local prices, and again to a falling exchange rate.


This is why doing nothing is not actually the safe option many assume it to be. Holding all your money in idle cash during a period of high inflation and a weakening currency is a slow, near-guaranteed loss of purchasing power. The instinct to keep money “safe” in the bank can quietly cost you.


## How inflation affects your investments


Investments respond to inflation differently from cash, and that difference is the whole point. Shares represent ownership in real businesses, and many companies can raise their prices as costs rise, which means their revenues and profits can grow in an inflationary environment in a way that idle cash simply cannot.


That is the reasoning behind why equities are often held as a long-term response to inflation: over long periods, ownership of productive businesses has tended to hold value better than cash. Some kinds of companies cope better than others. Businesses with strong brands and pricing power, or those whose earnings are tied to rising prices, can pass higher costs on to customers. Others, with thin margins or heavy debt, can struggle when inflation pushes up their costs faster than their revenues.


It is important to be clear-eyed here. Investing is not an automatic or guaranteed shield against inflation. Share prices fall as well as rise, some companies handle inflation badly, and there are periods when markets and inflation move against investors at the same time. What investing offers is not a guarantee, but a chance to grow your money at a rate that can keep pace with or outrun rising prices over the long term, which cash on its own cannot do.


## How naira devaluation affects your investments


Devaluation matters most through the currency your investments are held in. Assets priced in naira lose value in dollar terms when the naira weakens, while assets priced in dollars gain value in naira terms over the same period.


Think about what that means in practice. If all your wealth is in naira, a falling naira erodes its international value even if the naira amount stays the same. But if you hold some assets priced in dollars, a weaker naira actually increases their value when measured back in naira. This is the single biggest reason many Nigerians hold some of their investments in dollar-denominated assets: it gives them exposure to a currency that has, over recent years, held its value far better than the naira. If you are investing from outside Nigeria, the currency dynamics work differently again, and our guide to[investing in the NGX from abroad](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-nigerians-abroad-can-invest-in-ngx-stocks/) covers that case.


This is where US stocks come in for a lot of Nigerian investors. Because[US stocks on Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/us-stocks) are priced in dollars, holding them gives a naira-based investor exposure to dollar assets. When the naira weakens against the dollar, the naira value of those holdings rises, all else being equal.


The honest caveat matters as much as the point. Currency exposure cuts both ways: if the naira strengthens, as it has done at times in 2026, the effect works in reverse and dollar assets are worth less in naira. US stocks also carry their own market risk entirely separate from currency, so they can fall in dollar terms too. Dollar exposure is a way to diversify the currency risk in your portfolio, not a one-way bet.


## So what can you actually do about it?


The practical response to inflation and devaluation is to put money to work rather than leave it idle, and to spread it across different types of assets. No single move removes the risk, but a few principles consistently help.


The first is simply to invest rather than hold everything in cash, so at least part of your money has the chance to grow faster than prices rise. The second is to diversify across both naira and dollar assets:[Nigerian stocks](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) give you ownership in the local economy and access to dividends, while dollar-denominated assets like US stocks give you exposure that can offset naira weakness. Holding both means you are not fully exposed to either the naira falling or the local market alone, which is also part of[weathering a market downturn](https://learn.investbamboo.com/what-happens-to-your-investments-in-a-market-downturn/) . The third is to think in years, not weeks, because the case for investing through inflation rests on the long term, not on short-term timing.


What this looks like for you specifically depends on your goals, your time horizon, and how much risk you can take, which is why this is general information rather than a recommendation. But the underlying logic is sound: in an environment where cash loses value on two fronts, doing nothing has a cost, and a diversified, long-term approach is how many Nigerians try to protect and grow what they have.


## A balanced view


It is worth ending on the caveats, because the goal here is clear thinking, not a sales pitch for any asset. Investing is not a guaranteed hedge against inflation or devaluation. Stock markets fall, sometimes sharply and for long stretches. Dollar assets can lose value in naira terms when the naira strengthens, and they carry market risk of their own. And no one can reliably predict where inflation or the exchange rate goes next.


What is reasonably clear is the alternative. Leaving all your money in idle cash during sustained high inflation and currency weakness is one of the few near-certain ways to lose purchasing power over time. Investing carries risk and offers no guarantees, but it at least gives your money a chance to keep up. The sensible path is a considered, diversified, long-term one, made with money you can afford to leave invested and, if you are unsure, with advice from a professional.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does inflation reduce the value of my savings?** Yes, in real terms, whenever inflation is higher than the interest your savings earn. If prices rise by around 16% while your account earns 8%, your money grows on paper but buys less over time. That gap is your real loss.


**How does a weaker naira affect my investments?** Assets held in naira lose value against the dollar when the naira falls, while assets priced in dollars, such as US stocks, gain value in naira terms. This is why many Nigerians hold some dollar-denominated investments to offset naira weakness.


**Can investing protect me from inflation?** Investing can help, because ownership of real businesses has historically tended to keep pace with or outrun inflation over the long term, which cash cannot. But it is not guaranteed. Share prices fall as well as rise, and there is no certain hedge.


**Should I keep my money in dollars instead of naira?** Holding some dollar-denominated assets can diversify your currency risk, but currency exposure cuts both ways, and dollar assets carry their own market risk. A mix of naira and dollar assets is how many investors balance this, rather than going all in on either.


**Is it better to invest or leave my money in the bank during high inflation?** Leaving all your money in idle cash during high inflation means it steadily loses purchasing power. Investing carries risk and no guarantees, but it gives your money a chance to grow faster than prices. What suits you depends on your goals and risk tolerance.

### Quick Summary


This guide explains how inflation and naira devaluation affect your investments in Nigeria. Inflation, which stood at 15.91% in June 2026, erodes the purchasing power of money, so cash held in savings that earn less than the inflation rate loses real value over time. Naira devaluation, from around ₦460 to the US dollar in 2023 to roughly ₦1,400 in 2026 after the currency was floated, reduces the value of naira-denominated wealth against imports and foreign currency. In response, many Nigerians invest rather than hold idle cash, and diversify across both naira assets such as NGX stocks and dollar-denominated assets such as US stocks, which can offset naira weakness. Investing is not a guaranteed hedge: markets can fall, currency movements cut both ways, and returns are never guaranteed. This is general information, not investment advice.
